What is a mind?

A shared study of thinking, feeling, making, and being.

MIND(s) proposes a common first-year encounter with great works that examine mind across languages and cultures. It brings neuroscience into conversation with philosophy, Asian Studies, music, poetry, art, psychology, and sport.

Students would study minds through evidence, interpretation, and practice—and learn to write clearly about what remains unsettled.

Before Gutenberg: directly pointing to mind

Begin with Jikji →

The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type is a book about mind. Printed in Korea in 1377, Jikji brings Buddhist teachings and the history of books directly into MIND(s). Its English title: Essential Passages Pointing Directly to the Mind.

Hear words for mind.

Explore the human-voice collection →

Languages connect thinking, feeling and understanding in different ways. Listen to individual speakers and compare the words. Explore meaning clusters, sign languages and visual representations of mind.

One theme. Many ways of knowing.

See the ten-week sequence →

Thinking & feeling

Neuroscience, philosophy and psychology distinguish attention, intelligence, affect and conscious experience. Students learn what each method can establish.

Practice & perception

Asian Studies, sport and music bring trained action, cultivation, ensemble coordination and bodily experience into the center of the course.

Form & imagination

Poetry and art develop their own accounts of experience. Close reading, listening and looking receive the same care as scientific interpretation.

Three starting points in current research

Browse all sources →

Michael Levin

Coordination beyond the brain

Cellular organization expands the study of cognition. The distinction between adaptive behavior and felt experience remains crucial.

Read the sources

Mark Solms

Feeling at the center

An affect-centered account connects consciousness to bodily needs and uncertainty. Its extension to artificial agents is an active research claim.

Read the sources

Cameron Berg

Evidence from artificial systems

Mechanistic probes and model behavior make AI consciousness a concrete research problem. Self-report is a finding to examine, not a verdict.

Read the sources

These are initial research priorities. The learning bank also includes competing theories, empirical tests, and cultural works. Inclusion does not imply agreement or endorsement.

A liberal arts course about the minds doing the learning.

The strongest case for MIND(s) is curricular: students can practice several kinds of inquiry on a shared subject that matters to their own intellectual lives.

A musician can bring the structure of a performance. An athlete can bring trained perception. A poet can bring an exact distinction that ordinary language misses. A scientist can bring a testable prediction. Each contribution changes the conversation.

The model centers sustained reading across Chinese, Buddhist, Islamic, European, African American and Japanese contexts, with a progression from summary through synthesis and revision. It treats disagreement as something to describe precisely.

A possible planning horizon

Lawrence’s June 2024 announcement describes Water as a four-year theme beginning in fall 2024. The current works page labels the theme 2024–27. These public descriptions need clarification before proposing a transition date.

The transition date, proposal deadline and decision process still need confirmation.
